narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 50.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your undergraduate GPA was the single strongest factor, and it worked in your favor: at 3.40 it sits noticeably above the average of students who were admitted, pulling the prediction toward eventual success on the bar. Unfortunately, two other factors outweighed that advantage. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the second most influential piece of information and pushed strongly toward failure; you placed in the second decile while admitted students typically ranked around the sixth. Your first-year ranking was the third most important factor and also pointed toward failure, again landing you in the second decile compared with an average of sixth among those who were accepted.

Taken together, the model saw your early and later law-school performance as stronger signals of bar-exam risk than your solid college grades. The family income bracket and LSAT score played smaller roles and did not change the outcome.

You should focus on strengthening your academic standing in the remaining years, seek targeted bar-prep support early, and consider reapplying once you have improved your class rank. Many students in similar situations have succeeded on a second attempt after addressing these exact gaps. (248 words)
